findings.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The blocked_emails table and BlockedEmail model ship with no writer anywhere in the diff — no admin UI, rake task, seed, or API path creates BlockedEmail records. Operators cannot actually block any email address short of dropping into a Rails console; the entire feature is inert in production until a separate, not-yet-existing management surface is built.

[ADVISORY] BlockedEmail.should_block? performs record.save (a DB UPDATE of match_count/last_match_at) from inside model validation on every email change, and the integer counter write is not guarded against concurrent races. Every user save with a changed email that matches a blocked record issues an UPDATE inside validation (before the record itself is validated as a whole), and concurrent registrations on the same blocked email produce lost match_count increments; a failed save of the stats row silently still allows the block decision to proceed based on the in-memory record.

[ADVISORY] The new `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?` resolves the validator by const lookup, but EmailValidator lives in lib/validators/, a path that is only loaded if lib is in Rails autoload_paths/eager_load_paths. If lib (or lib/validators) is not on the autoload path in this app's configuration, `validates :email, email: true` raises NameError at class load time, breaking every request that touches User; verify lib/ is in config.autoload_paths before merge.

[BUG] The whitelist/blacklist half of validate_each is duplicated verbatim from the deleted User#email_validator, including its original defect that the domain restriction regex is built from the raw setting with only dots escaped, so a domain list containing regex metacharacters (e.g. 'foo+bar.com') produces an invalid or wrong Regexp. A site admin whose email_domains_blacklist/whitelist contains '+' or other regex metacharacters gets a RegexpError raised during user validation (500 on signup) instead of a domain match; the move to the shared validator preserves the bug and now also applies it to any other model that uses `validates email: true`.

[ADVISORY] The client-side rejectedEmails check compares the raw typed string against the server-returned rejected email, but the server-side uniqueness/presence checks and BlockedEmail lookup are case-insensitive at the DB level (MySQL/PG citext or lower-case comparisons vary), and an email rejected once is rejected for exact matches only. A user whose 'User@Spam.com' was rejected gets the instant inline 'invalid' message when retyping the identical string, but changing case ('user@spam.com') bypasses the client check and resubmits to the server, producing a flash error instead of inline feedback — inconsistent UX, and the property dependency `rejectedEmails.@each` correctly re-fires only for the exact string.

[ADVISORY] The domain whitelist/blacklist restriction logic moved from user.rb into EmailValidator but no spec in this diff exercises the whitelist or blacklist paths — the new spec stubs BlockedEmail.should_block? and never sets SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist/blacklist. A regression in the transplanted regex/gsub restriction logic (e.g. the escaping of dots or the elsif ordering) would silently stop rejecting disallowed email domains, and no test in this diff would fail; the only assertions cover the blocked-list branch.

[ADVISORY] BlockedEmail.should_block? does an exact string lookup with no case normalization, while nothing in the diff downcases the email before comparison. A user registering with Bad@spamclub.com bypasses a blocked_email row stored as bad@spamclub.com, so the block feature is defeated by capitalizing any letter of the address; who gets bitten: any operator relying on the blocked list.

[ADVISORY] should_block? performs a read-modify-write (record.save) inside model validation, mutating match_count and last_match_at every time any record's email is validated, including failed validations and repeat attempts. Operators see inflated match_count stats from retries and from validations of records that never save, and every create-account attempt now incurs a write on the blocked_emails row from inside the validation path; also the stats are not updated when a domain-restriction error was already added (errors blank guard), so counts are inconsistent.

[ADVISORY] The blocked_emails table and BlockedEmail model ship with no writer anywhere in this diff — no admin UI, API endpoint, rake task, or seed populates it. Operators cannot actually add blocked emails without hand-crafting SQL, making the entire block feature inert until a follow-up lands; also the case-sensitive unique index on email is unindexed for the lookup beyond the unique index, which does serve it, but the operational gap stands.

[ADVISORY] The client pushes result.values.email into rejectedEmails only when both result.errors and result.values are present, and the JS check reuses the generic user.email.invalid message rather than the server's specific blocked message. Against an older server (or any error response without values) the email is never added to rejectedEmails, so the inline validation silently does nothing after a failed submit; and users whose email is blocked see 'is invalid' instead of the distinct user.email.blocked reason, hiding why the address was refused.

[ADVISORY] The spec calls validate_each directly with a Fabricate-built user, bypassing the if: :email_changed? conditional that the model applies, so the conditional wiring (email format/block validation only when email changed) is untested. If the if: condition or the validates :email, email: true declaration regresses (e.g. condition dropped or attribute misspelled), blocked emails would stop being rejected at signup and no test in this diff would fail.

[ADVISORY] BlockedEmail.should_block? performs a write (increment match_count, set last_match_at, save) inside a validation path, which is statistics-tracking functionality not traceable to the stated intent of blocking signups. Every failed signup attempt with a matching email triggers an extra UPDATE plus a second query; admins on high-spam sites see DB churn from bot traffic, and a concurrent save failure inside the validator turns a should-be-4xx signup into an exception path. Operators who only want blocking get unasked-for analytics writes.

[ADVISORY] The BlockedEmail table is a ships-inert feature: nothing in this diff outside specs writes to it — no admin UI, rake task, seed, or API endpoint inserts BlockedEmail records. Operators deploying this PR cannot populate the blocklist at all; the blocked-email validation can never fire in production until unrelated tooling is written, so the feature's stated intent is unenforceable by the shipped code.

[ADVISORY] The controller change is scope drift: returning full error hashes and echoed user attributes (name, username, email) on every failed create is a new generic error API shaped to serve this one client-side feature. Every future failure response now leaks the server's internal error structure and echoes arbitrary submitted values back to any API consumer, expanding the public contract beyond what blocking emails requires; the client only consumes errors.email and values.email.

[ADVISORY] The PR bundles a behavioral refactor of existing email validation (replacing presence/uniqueness/email_validator with the new EmailValidator) that is only incidentally related to the blocked-emails intent. The rename/reorder silently changes validation sequence and semantics for all existing signup paths (e.g. uniqueness now validates via validates rather than validates_uniqueness_of, and the whitelist/blacklist check moved into an EachValidator that only runs on non-nil values), so regressions in the pre-existing whitelist/blacklist behavior land in a PR whose stated intent is only blocked-user validation, with no spec in this diff covering the migrated whitelist/blacklist paths.

[BUG] BlockedEmail.should_block? performs a read-modify-write on match_count with no atomic increment or lock, and it is invoked from inside User validation on every save attempt. Concurrent signup attempts for the same blocked email both read match_count=N and both write N+1, losing counts; worse, the write fires inside a validation pass that may run multiple times per request (controller valid?/save), so match_count/last_match_at statistics are double-counted and inflated, defeating their stated purpose of tracking how often an email was blocked.

[ADVISORY] A validation method triggers a database write (BlockedEmail#save inside should_block?) as a side effect of validating an unsaved User. The blocked-email stat row is committed even when the surrounding User save fails or the transaction rolls back, so last_match_at/match_count record 'blocks' that never resulted in a rejected signup; the audit trail is written out-of-transaction relative to the user creation it purports to measure.

[BUG] BlockedEmail lookup compares email case-sensitively (where(email: email) on Postgres) while the blocked list is loaded by hand with no canonicalization, and no downcase is applied on either write or read. An operator inserting 'Spam@Example.com' into blocked_emails (the only population path) never matches a user registering 'spam@example.com', so the block silently fails; the unique index likewise permits 'a@x.com' and 'A@x.com' as distinct blocked rows.

[ADVISORY] The email validator (including the blocked-email check) only runs when email_changed?, and only on the User model — no other email-ingestion path validates. Invites, admin-created users via other flows, or email updates that dodge email_changed? bypass the blocked list entirely; parallel service paths mean blocked emails can still enter the system through invite-based signup, which creates a User without running this validation chain in the same way.

[ADVISORY] The blocked_emails table ships with no writer anywhere in the diff — no admin UI, API endpoint, rake task, or seed populates it. Operators cannot actually use the feature: the only way to block an email is direct SQL/console, so the 'comprehensive email validation for blocked users' advertised by the PR is inert in production until a separate, unreviewed population path is built.

[BUG] The client rejects future attempts by exact string match rejectedEmails.contains(email) against result.values.email (the server-side attribute), while the user's typed accountEmail may differ in case. A user whose signup failed with a blocked-email error and who retypes the address with different casing (or whose input was normalized server-side before being echoed back in values) gets no client-side rejection — the form re-submits to the server instead of failing fast, and the client-side cache silently misses.

[ADVISORY] The client-side rejection reuses the 'user.email.invalid' message for what is actually a blocked/not-allowed condition, while the server defines a distinct 'user.email.blocked' string. End users who were blocked see 'invalid email' copy that misdescribes the actual reason (and the client never surfaces the server's specific error message for the email field), and the two locales will drift as copy evolves.

[ADVISORY] should_block? is a boolean-named predicate that mutates persistent state (increments match_count, updates last_match_at, saves) — the name promises a query while performing a write. Any future caller invoking should_block? for a read-only check (e.g., in a view, a rake report, or a pre-flight API probe) silently increments statistics; the next developer treating it as a query gets corrupted analytics.

[BUG] BlockedEmail.should_block? does an exact case-sensitive string match against the stored email, so a blocked address is bypassed by any case variant of the local part or domain. A spammer blocked as 'bad@spammers.org' registers as 'Bad@Spammers.ORG' and passes the new 'blocked' validation that this PR's whole purpose is to enforce; the check intended to stop them returns false and the account is created.

[BUG] The client-side rejection path reuses I18n.t('user.email.invalid') for emails the server rejected as blocked, discarding the specific server message ('user.email.blocked' / 'not_allowed') that the users_controller now returns. A user whose email is blocked by an admin sees the generic invalid-email message, concludes the address is malformed, and retries the same address or abandons signup instead of learning to use another address; the new 'blocked' locale string added in this same diff never reaches the user.

[ADVISORY] The blocked-email check runs inside the shared EmailValidator with `if: :email_changed?` inherited from User's `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?`, but also fires on every other model that later adopts this validator. The match_count/last_match_at statistics are incremented by validation runs that are not real signup attempts (e.g. double validation passes within one request, or any future model using this validator), so admins reading 'how often has this address tried' get inflated counts; the test comment in blocked_email_spec.rb documents last_match_at as the signal for 'ever been blocked', which the side-effect placement corrupts.

[ADVISORY] should_block? mutates and saves the record inside a predicate invoked from validation, so a query-shaped method performs a synchronous write on every email validation. Any code path that validates a user with a changed email (admin edits, updates from other controllers) now silently issues an UPDATE on blocked_emails; a failed save inside validation raises inside the validation pass and surfaces as an opaque validation error, and the write happens even when the validation result is discarded (e.g. .invalid? probes).

[ADVISORY] The blocked_emails table is created with no writer anywhere in this diff — no admin UI, API endpoint, rake task, or seed populates it. Operators deploying this feature cannot add a single blocked email without hand-written SQL, so the 'comprehensive email validation for blocked users' the PR promises is inert in production until follow-up work lands; the shipped feature silently does nothing.

[ADVISORY] The controller echoes back user.attributes including the raw email in `values` on the failure response, and the client pushes only values.email into rejectedEmails without ever clearing that list on modal close. A user who fails signup with a blocked email, closes the modal, changes their mind and types the same address gets a client-side 'invalid' error that can never be cleared by retyping — the stale rejectedEmails entry persists for the controller's lifetime and blocks an address the server may not even reject after an admin unblocks it, until a full page reload.

[BUG] BlockedEmail.should_block? performs a case-sensitive exact-match lookup on an unnormalized email, so a blocked address is trivially bypassed by varying letter case. An admin blocks 'spammer@evil.com'; the spammer registers 'Spammer@evil.com' (or 'SPAMMER@EVIL.COM') and the WHERE email = ... clause on Postgres returns no row, so should_block? returns false and the account is created — the entire feature is defeated by holding the shift key.

[BUG] email_in_restriction_setting? interpolates the raw admin-configured domain string into Regexp.new with no escaping of regex metacharacters, and the resulting pattern is unanchored on the right. A whitelist entry 'gmail.com' builds /@(gmail\.com)/i which matches 'user@gmail.com.attacker.org', letting any attacker-controlled domain pass the whitelist; additionally an entry containing an unbalanced '(' (e.g. 'foo(bar.com') raises RegexpError inside validation, turning every account creation / email change into a 500 until an admin fixes the setting — config is attacker-controllable input (any admin, or a compromised admin panel) feeding a regex sink.

[ADVISORY] should_block? mutates and saves the BlockedEmail row during model validation, doing a write (with a unique-index conflict risk under concurrency) on every candidate-email validation attempt. Two concurrent signups with the same blocked email race on record.save; on Postgres the second save raises a unique-constraint StatementInvalid, which users_controller rescues only as a generic rescue rendering an opaque error. Unauthenticated attackers also inflate match_count arbitrarily via repeated signup attempts, corrupting the stats the model was built to collect; and the write happens during email-change validation for existing users too, not just signup.

[ADVISORY] The email uniqueness validation is now a plain Rails uniqueness check with no case-insensitive scope or downcasing, combined with the removal of the dedicated email_validator method means case-variant duplicate emails are never blocked at the app layer. If the DB unique index on users.email is case-sensitive (Postgres default), 'Bob@x.com' and 'bob@x.com' both validate as unique, producing duplicate accounts for one mailbox — an account-recovery/impersonation foothold for shared-mailbox domains; the index schema is not added or altered in this diff to enforce case-insensitivity.

[ADVISORY] The failure response now echoes user-supplied values (name, username, email) back in the JSON payload, which the client pushes into client-side state and re-displays via the error flash path. Any XSS sink that renders result.values.email or the flash message without escaping turns the signup form into a reflected/stored XSS vector via the server-echoed email field; safe only as long as every consuming template escapes, which this diff does not verify.

[ADVISORY] The EmailValidator spec covers only the BlockedEmail branch of validate_each and leaves the whitelist/blacklist branches (lib/validators/email_validator.rb lines 5-14, the majority of the validator's logic) with zero coverage in this diff. A regression in email_in_restriction_setting? (e.g. the dot-escaping regexp gsub, which is subtle string interpolation into Regexp.new) ships green because the spec suite never constructs a SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist/blacklist case; admins relying on domain restrictions get users signed up from blacklisted domains before anyone notices. Checked spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb and spec/models/blocked_email_spec.rb — neither sets either SiteSetting.

[ADVISORY] Both specs stub BlockedEmail.should_block? with a canned return value, so the test pair is a tautology that verifies only that an if-statement branches on a stubbed boolean — the real BlockedEmail query, the action_type comparison, and the 'user.email.blocked' message are never exercised through the validator. spec/models/blocked_email_spec.rb covers should_block? in isolation, but the wiring between validator and model is never integration-tested: if the validator's errors message key changes or the errors[attribute].blank? guard misfires in the presence of a pre-existing error, these specs still pass while end-to-end blocked-email rejection is broken. The specs also assert only errors present/absent, never the message content, so a wrong I18n key passes.

[ADVISORY] No test exercises the combined branch where a whitelist/blacklist error is already present so BlockedEmail.should_block? is short-circuited (lib/validators/email_validator.rb line 15 'if record.errors[attribute].blank and ...'), meaning the behavioral side effect — match_count not incremented and last_match_at not updated when the domain restriction fires first — is unverified. Site operators loading the blocked_emails table to track which blocked addresses are being attempted (the explicit rationale in the last_match_at spec comment) get silently wrong statistics for any email that also trips a domain restriction, and no spec fails to reveal it. Checked both spec files in the diff; neither creates a record with both a domain restriction error and a blocked email.

[ADVISORY] The new blocked_emails table has no writer anywhere in this diff, and its action_type column is NOT NULL with no database default. Operators who want to use the feature must hand-load rows via SQL (the spec comment explicitly anticipates 'manually load the table'), and any raw INSERT that omits action_type fails on the NOT NULL constraint because the default only exists in the model's before_validation callback; meanwhile no admin UI/API exists to populate the table, so the feature ships inert.

[ADVISORY] BlockedEmail.should_block? performs a read-modify-write save inside a validation path, and is invoked from EmailValidator on every email_changed? validation. Every signup validation run (including repeated .valid? calls in one request or controller) increments match_count and issues an UPDATE, so statistics are double-counted and a hot signup path gains an unconditional DB write per attempt; a failure of that save (e.g., unique-index race) raises inside validation and turns a rejection into a 500.

[ADVISORY] BlockedEmail lookup matches the raw email string exactly with no normalization, while email_in_restriction_setting? uses a case-insensitive regexp. A user entering Blocked@Spammers.org when the table contains blocked@spammers.org is accepted (no match), so manually-loaded blocklists silently miss case variants; also, since case-insensitive uniqueness on users.email elsewhere in the codebase means the same person registers the same address in different casing, the blocklist is only as good as the exact string loaded.

[BUG] BlockedEmail.should_block? performs a stateful DB write (incrementing match_count, setting last_match_at, record.save) inside User's validation pass, so the write runs on every validation, not on the actual blocked event. A single failed signup for a blocked email gets counted once per validation pass (validations run multiple times across form re-submissions and other code paths that call valid?/save), inflating match_count and rewriting last_match_at; additionally, since should_block? is invoked from validate_each, the UPDATE executes inside the surrounding user-save transaction and is silently rolled back when the user creation fails for any other reason — the stats write is silently dropped (record.save's return value is never checked) with no log or error.

[ADVISORY] The match_count increment uses read-modify-write (record.match_count += 1; record.save) with no locking, so concurrent signup attempts for the same blocked email lose increments. Operators relying on match_count to gauge spam pressure under-count under concurrency (two simultaneous requests both read count=5, both write 6); also the concurrent saves can collide on updated_at/last_match_at, last write wins. Low impact for stats, but the counter's purpose (measuring abuse volume) is exactly the workload where concurrency occurs.

[ADVISORY] The client-side rejectedEmails check only fires after a failed submit and displays the generic I18n.t('user.email.invalid') message rather than the server's specific 'user.email.blocked' message delivered in result.errors.email. A user whose email is blocked on a retry sees 'invalid' (generic format message) instead of the server's 'is not allowed.' message that was already returned in the payload, misleading the user into thinking they typo'd the address and retrying format changes that can never succeed.

[ADVISORY] The create-failure response now unconditionally includes user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email"), echoing the user's raw submitted email back in every failed-signup response regardless of which field failed. Callers get the submitted email echoed even when the failure was a username/password error, which the client only consumes on email errors; more importantly the response payload grows per-request with unvalidated input on an unauthenticated endpoint (previously only the message was returned). Minor, but it is a new unbounded-ish echo of raw input on the public signup path.

goldens.comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.

The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces `blocked_emails` (migration), `BlockedEmail` model, and enforces blocking via the new `EmailValidator` (`BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`), but within the shown changes there is no UI/controller/rake task/seed/API added that would let operators create/manage `BlockedEmail` records. As a result, with only this diff applied, the blocking mechanism will never trigger unless records are inserted out-of-band (e.g., console/DB). This is an incomplete feature surface rather than a runtime defect in the added code paths.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a custom ActiveModel validator in `lib/validators/email_validator.rb` and immediately relies on it via `validates :email, email: true` in `app/models/user.rb`. Whether Rails will autoload `EmailValidator` from `lib/validators` depends on app configuration (`autoload_paths`/`eager_load_paths`), which is not shown in the diff. This makes the review note a concrete, diff-grounded integration risk, but not a verifiable defect from the provided changes alone.

adjudication.rationale: In `lib/validators/email_validator.rb`, `email_in_restriction_setting?` constructs `Regexp.new("@(#{domains})", true)` after only escaping dots via `setting.gsub('.', '\.')`. Any other regexp metacharacters present in the admin-provided setting (e.g. `+`, `(`, `]`, `\`) will be interpreted as regex syntax, leading to incorrect matching and potentially `RegexpError` for invalid patterns. This logic is copied from the deleted `User#email_in_restriction_setting?`, so the defect persists and is now part of the shared `EmailValidator` used by `User` (and potentially other models).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The client-side rejectedEmails check compares the raw typed string against the server-returned rejected email, but the server-side uniqueness/presence checks and BlockedEmail lookup are case-insensitive at the DB level (MySQL/PG citext or lower-case comparisons vary), and an email rejected once is rejected for exact matches only. A user whose 'User@Spam.com' was rejected gets the instant inline 'invalid' message when retyping the identical string, but changing case ('user@spam.com') bypasses the client check and resubmits to the server, producing a flash error instead of inline feedback — inconsistent UX, and the property dependency `rejectedEmails.@each` correctly re-fires only for the exact string.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does show that `rejectedEmails.contains(email)` is an exact-string client-side check (create_account_controller.js) and that rejected emails are pushed from `result.values.email`. However, the finding’s core premise—that server-side uniqueness/blocked-email checks are case-insensitive (e.g., MySQL collation, PG citext, or explicit lowercasing) and therefore case changes would still be rejected server-side—is not established anywhere in the diff. Rails `validates :email, uniqueness: true` is case-sensitive by default unless configured otherwise, and `BlockedEmail.where(email: email)` is also case-sensitive absent DB/citext details not shown. So the described “case-change bypasses client check but still fails on server” behavior cannot be verified from this PR diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The domain whitelist/blacklist restriction logic moved from user.rb into EmailValidator but no spec in this diff exercises the whitelist or blacklist paths — the new spec stubs BlockedEmail.should_block? and never sets SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist/blacklist. A regression in the transplanted regex/gsub restriction logic (e.g. the escaping of dots or the elsif ordering) would silently stop rejecting disallowed email domains, and no test in this diff would fail; the only assertions cover the blocked-list branch.

adjudication.rationale: The diff moves the domain whitelist/blacklist restriction logic out of `User#email_validator` (removed in `app/models/user.rb`) into the new `lib/validators/email_validator.rb` (`email_in_restriction_setting?`, the whitelist/blacklist `if/elsif` branches). The only added validator spec (`spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb`) stubs `BlockedEmail.should_block?` and asserts presence/absence of errors solely for the blocked-email branch; it never sets `SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist` or `SiteSetting.email_domains_blacklist`, so the transplanted restriction logic is untested in this diff and could regress without failing tests.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] BlockedEmail.should_block? does an exact string lookup with no case normalization, while nothing in the diff downcases the email before comparison. A user registering with Bad@spamclub.com bypasses a blocked_email row stored as bad@spamclub.com, so the block feature is defeated by capitalizing any letter of the address; who gets bitten: any operator relying on the blocked list.

[ADVISORY] should_block? performs a read-modify-write (record.save) inside model validation, mutating match_count and last_match_at every time any record's email is validated, including failed validations and repeat attempts. Operators see inflated match_count stats from retries and from validations of records that never save, and every create-account attempt now incurs a write on the blocked_emails row from inside the validation path; also the stats are not updated when a domain-restriction error was already added (errors blank guard), so counts are inconsistent.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds EmailValidator#validate_each, which calls BlockedEmail.should_block?(value) during model validation when no prior email error exists (record.errors[attribute].blank?). BlockedEmail.should_block? does a read-modify-write (increments match_count, sets last_match_at, record.save) any time a matching blocked_emails row exists, regardless of whether the User ultimately saves or whether the validation fails later for other reasons. This introduces side effects and extra DB writes on the validation path, and the guard means blocked-email stats are skipped when whitelist/blacklist has already added an error, making counts inconsistent. These are real, diff-grounded concerns, but they primarily affect metrics/perf/side-effect semantics rather than breaking core correctness.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The blocked_emails table and BlockedEmail model ship with no writer anywhere in this diff — no admin UI, API endpoint, rake task, or seed populates it. Operators cannot actually add blocked emails without hand-crafting SQL, making the entire block feature inert until a follow-up lands; also the case-sensitive unique index on email is unindexed for the lookup beyond the unique index, which does serve it, but the operational gap stands.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a `blocked_emails` table/migration and a `BlockedEmail` model used by the new `EmailValidator` (`BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`), but within this diff there is no code path that creates or manages `BlockedEmail` records outside of tests/fabricators. That makes the feature operationally incomplete unless operators manually insert rows. The note about the lookup being “unindexed beyond the unique index” is off (the unique index on `email` would serve the `where(email: ...)` query), but the core gap (no writer/admin/API/seed in this diff) is diff-grounded.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The client pushes result.values.email into rejectedEmails only when both result.errors and result.values are present, and the JS check reuses the generic user.email.invalid message rather than the server's specific blocked message. Against an older server (or any error response without values) the email is never added to rejectedEmails, so the inline validation silently does nothing after a failed submit; and users whose email is blocked see 'is invalid' instead of the distinct user.email.blocked reason, hiding why the address was refused.

adjudication.rationale: In create_account_controller.js, the inline email validation short-circuits on `rejectedEmails.contains(email)` but always returns `I18n.t('user.email.invalid')` (not the more specific server-side `user.email.blocked` added in server.en.yml and used by the new EmailValidator). Also, the client only pushes into `rejectedEmails` when `result.errors && result.errors.email && result.values`; while this PR’s users_controller.rb now includes `errors` and `values` in the failure JSON, the client-side condition does create a compatibility/edge-case gap for any error responses lacking `values`. This is a concrete diff-grounded UX/edge-case issue, but not a clear correctness break within the PR’s updated server+client behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The spec calls validate_each directly with a Fabricate-built user, bypassing the if: :email_changed? conditional that the model applies, so the conditional wiring (email format/block validation only when email changed) is untested. If the if: condition or the validates :email, email: true declaration regresses (e.g. condition dropped or attribute misspelled), blocked emails would stop being rejected at signup and no test in this diff would fail.

adjudication.rationale: In `User` the new validator is wired as `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?` (user.rb), but the added spec `spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb` instantiates `EmailValidator` and calls `validate_each` directly on a fabricated `User`. That tests the validator logic in isolation, not the model-level conditional/wiring (e.g., that the `email:` validator actually runs only when `email_changed?` and is correctly attached to `:email`). A regression in the `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?` line could break signup blocking without this spec failing.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] BlockedEmail.should_block? performs a write (increment match_count, set last_match_at, save) inside a validation path, which is statistics-tracking functionality not traceable to the stated intent of blocking signups. Every failed signup attempt with a matching email triggers an extra UPDATE plus a second query; admins on high-spam sites see DB churn from bot traffic, and a concurrent save failure inside the validator turns a should-be-4xx signup into an exception path. Operators who only want blocking get unasked-for analytics writes.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `EmailValidator#validate_each` calling `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` when no other email errors exist (lib/validators/email_validator.rb). `BlockedEmail.should_block?` performs a read (`where(email: email).first`) and, on match, writes stats (`match_count += 1`, `last_match_at = Time.zone.now`, `record.save`) (app/models/blocked_email.rb). This means validating a signup email can trigger an UPDATE (and any associated failure/latency) even though the validator’s primary purpose is allow/deny. That’s a concrete diff-grounded performance/architecture concern, not a guaranteed functional defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The BlockedEmail table is a ships-inert feature: nothing in this diff outside specs writes to it — no admin UI, rake task, seed, or API endpoint inserts BlockedEmail records. Operators deploying this PR cannot populate the blocklist at all; the blocked-email validation can never fire in production until unrelated tooling is written, so the feature's stated intent is unenforceable by the shipped code.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces `BlockedEmail` (model + migration) and enforces it via `EmailValidator` (`BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` in `lib/validators/email_validator.rb`), but the only places creating `BlockedEmail` records in this diff are test helpers/specs (`spec/fabricators/blocked_email_fabricator.rb`, specs that `Fabricate(:blocked_email)`). There is no production/admin/API/seed/rake code shown here that inserts or manages `blocked_emails`, so in normal operation the blocklist would stay empty unless operators manually insert rows outside the shipped app code (e.g., via console/SQL). That makes the feature operationally incomplete, though not a correctness bug in the validation logic itself.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The controller change is scope drift: returning full error hashes and echoed user attributes (name, username, email) on every failed create is a new generic error API shaped to serve this one client-side feature. Every future failure response now leaks the server's internal error structure and echoes arbitrary submitted values back to any API consumer, expanding the public contract beyond what blocking emails requires; the client only consumes errors.email and values.email.

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes `UsersController#create` failure JSON from only `{success:false, message: ...}` to also include `errors: user.errors.to_hash` and `values: user.attributes.slice("name","username","email")` for every failed create (not just blocked-email failures). The client-side change only needs `result.errors.email` and `result.values.email` to populate `rejectedEmails`, so this does expand the public response contract and exposes Rails validation structure and echoed attributes more broadly than required by the feature.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The PR bundles a behavioral refactor of existing email validation (replacing presence/uniqueness/email_validator with the new EmailValidator) that is only incidentally related to the blocked-emails intent. The rename/reorder silently changes validation sequence and semantics for all existing signup paths (e.g. uniqueness now validates via validates rather than validates_uniqueness_of, and the whitelist/blacklist check moved into an EachValidator that only runs on non-nil values), so regressions in the pre-existing whitelist/blacklist behavior land in a PR whose stated intent is only blocked-user validation, with no spec in this diff covering the migrated whitelist/blacklist paths.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does bundle a broader refactor of pre-existing email validation into the blocked-email change: `User` removes the custom `email_validator` method and switches to `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?` using a new `EmailValidator` (lib/validators/email_validator.rb) that now also contains the whitelist/blacklist logic. The added specs cover only the new blocked-email branch (stubbing `BlockedEmail.should_block?`) and do not exercise the migrated whitelist/blacklist behavior, so regressions in that existing logic could land without coverage. While the finding claims some semantic changes that aren’t clearly verifiable from the diff alone, the scope/coverage concern is diff-grounded and actionable.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] BlockedEmail.should_block? performs a read-modify-write on match_count with no atomic increment or lock, and it is invoked from inside User validation on every save attempt. Concurrent signup attempts for the same blocked email both read match_count=N and both write N+1, losing counts; worse, the write fires inside a validation pass that may run multiple times per request (controller valid?/save), so match_count/last_match_at statistics are double-counted and inflated, defeating their stated purpose of tracking how often an email was blocked.

[ADVISORY] A validation method triggers a database write (BlockedEmail#save inside should_block?) as a side effect of validating an unsaved User. The blocked-email stat row is committed even when the surrounding User save fails or the transaction rolls back, so last_match_at/match_count record 'blocks' that never resulted in a rejected signup; the audit trail is written out-of-transaction relative to the user creation it purports to measure.

adjudication.rationale: Diff shows the new EmailValidator#validate_each calling BlockedEmail.should_block?(value) and only then adding an error (lib/validators/email_validator.rb). BlockedEmail.should_block? performs a DB write as a side effect (increments match_count, sets last_match_at, and record.save). That means merely validating a User (even before it is persisted, or in non-create validation contexts) can mutate blocked_email stats, which is a concrete design/architecture concern introduced here. However, the finding’s stronger claim that this write is definitively committed out-of-transaction even if the User save rolls back cannot be verified from the diff alone (Rails transaction boundaries aren’t shown), so it’s not provably a correctness bug from the patch itself.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] BlockedEmail lookup compares email case-sensitively (where(email: email) on Postgres) while the blocked list is loaded by hand with no canonicalization, and no downcase is applied on either write or read. An operator inserting 'Spam@Example.com' into blocked_emails (the only population path) never matches a user registering 'spam@example.com', so the block silently fails; the unique index likewise permits 'a@x.com' and 'A@x.com' as distinct blocked rows.

adjudication.rationale: In `BlockedEmail.should_block?(email)` the lookup is `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` with no canonicalization (`downcase`, etc.), and the migration creates a plain `string` column with a unique index on `:email` (not `citext` / functional lower index). As shown in the diff, this makes matching and uniqueness effectively case-sensitive on common DBs (e.g., Postgres), so `Spam@Example.com` and `spam@example.com` can be treated as different rows and a blocked entry may not match a differently-cased registration email.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The email validator (including the blocked-email check) only runs when email_changed?, and only on the User model — no other email-ingestion path validates. Invites, admin-created users via other flows, or email updates that dodge email_changed? bypass the blocked list entirely; parallel service paths mean blocked emails can still enter the system through invite-based signup, which creates a User without running this validation chain in the same way.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows the new blocked-email logic lives inside `EmailValidator` and is invoked from `User` via `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?` (app/models/user.rb). However, the claim that invite-based signup, admin-created users, or other ingestion paths “create a User without running this validation chain” is not verifiable from this PR diff: no invite/admin flows or alternative user-creation paths are shown. Also, `if: :email_changed?` already existed before (previously `validate :email_validator, if: :email_changed?`), and on new-record creation `email_changed?` would typically be true, so the blocked check would run for normal user creation.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The blocked_emails table ships with no writer anywhere in the diff — no admin UI, API endpoint, rake task, or seed populates it. Operators cannot actually use the feature: the only way to block an email is direct SQL/console, so the 'comprehensive email validation for blocked users' advertised by the PR is inert in production until a separate, unreviewed population path is built.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a `blocked_emails` table/model and wires it into `EmailValidator` via `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`, but it does not add any way (admin UI, API/controller, rake task, seeds) to create/manage `BlockedEmail` records. As shown, the feature exists only if operators manually insert rows (SQL/console), so it’s an incomplete operational surface rather than a runtime defect in the added logic.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The client rejects future attempts by exact string match rejectedEmails.contains(email) against result.values.email (the server-side attribute), while the user's typed accountEmail may differ in case. A user whose signup failed with a blocked-email error and who retypes the address with different casing (or whose input was normalized server-side before being echoed back in values) gets no client-side rejection — the form re-submits to the server instead of failing fast, and the client-side cache silently misses.

adjudication.rationale: In `create_account_controller.js`, the new fast-fail check is `this.get('rejectedEmails').contains(email)` where `email` is the current `accountEmail`, but the cached value is pushed from `result.values.email` (`rejectedEmails.pushObject(result.values.email)`). There is no normalization (e.g., downcasing/trim) on either side in this diff, so if the user re-enters the same address with different casing/formatting, the client-side cache can miss and the form will submit again. However, this doesn’t change ultimate correctness (the server-side validation still runs); it mainly reduces the effectiveness of the new client-side optimization rather than introducing a broken/unsafe behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The client-side rejection reuses the 'user.email.invalid' message for what is actually a blocked/not-allowed condition, while the server defines a distinct 'user.email.blocked' string. End users who were blocked see 'invalid email' copy that misdescribes the actual reason (and the client never surfaces the server's specific error message for the email field), and the two locales will drift as copy evolves.

adjudication.rationale: In `create_account_controller.js`, when an email is in `rejectedEmails`, the client returns a failed validation with `reason: I18n.t('user.email.invalid')`. However, the server-side validator explicitly adds a distinct blocked/not-allowed error via `I18n.t(:'user.email.blocked')` in `lib/validators/email_validator.rb` and the locale adds `user.email.blocked`. The controller also pushes rejected emails based on `result.errors.email` (`users_controller.rb` now returns `errors: user.errors.to_hash`), but the client never uses the server-provided specific email error text—so blocked emails will be reported to the user as “invalid” rather than “blocked/not allowed,” and the client/server copy can diverge.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] should_block? is a boolean-named predicate that mutates persistent state (increments match_count, updates last_match_at, saves) — the name promises a query while performing a write. Any future caller invoking should_block? for a read-only check (e.g., in a view, a rake report, or a pre-flight API probe) silently increments statistics; the next developer treating it as a query gets corrupted analytics.
matched_golden_ids: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate flags that a boolean/predicate method (`should_block?`) performs writes (increments counters, updates timestamps, saves), meaning a read/check operation has side effects and the name is misleading. This is the same core issue as the golden comment about `should_block_email?` updating statistics during a check, with associated risks like unintended state changes in concurrent/read-only usage.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] BlockedEmail.should_block? does an exact case-sensitive string match against the stored email, so a blocked address is bypassed by any case variant of the local part or domain. A spammer blocked as 'bad@spammers.org' registers as 'Bad@Spammers.ORG' and passes the new 'blocked' validation that this PR's whole purpose is to enforce; the check intended to stop them returns false and the account is created.

adjudication.rationale: In `BlockedEmail.should_block?(email)` the lookup is `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` with no normalization (e.g., `downcase`) and the DB column is a plain `string` with a unique index. From the diff alone, this means the blocked-email check is an exact equality match and therefore will not match case-variant inputs like `Bad@Spammers.ORG` when the stored row is `bad@spammers.org`, allowing the new `EmailValidator` (`BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`) to be bypassed.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The client-side rejection path reuses I18n.t('user.email.invalid') for emails the server rejected as blocked, discarding the specific server message ('user.email.blocked' / 'not_allowed') that the users_controller now returns. A user whose email is blocked by an admin sees the generic invalid-email message, concludes the address is malformed, and retries the same address or abandons signup instead of learning to use another address; the new 'blocked' locale string added in this same diff never reaches the user.

adjudication.rationale: In `create_account_controller.js`, when an email has previously been rejected, the validation short-circuits on `rejectedEmails.contains(email)` and returns `failed: true` with `reason: I18n.t('user.email.invalid')` (generic) rather than using the server-provided reason. The server now returns structured `errors` (including `user.email.blocked` / `user.email.not_allowed` from the new `EmailValidator`) and `values`, but the client only pushes `result.values.email` into `rejectedEmails` and discards `result.errors.email`. On subsequent attempts with the same blocked/not-allowed email, the user will see only the generic "invalid" message and will not see the more specific blocked/not_allowed message again.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The blocked-email check runs inside the shared EmailValidator with `if: :email_changed?` inherited from User's `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?`, but also fires on every other model that later adopts this validator. The match_count/last_match_at statistics are incremented by validation runs that are not real signup attempts (e.g. double validation passes within one request, or any future model using this validator), so admins reading 'how often has this address tried' get inflated counts; the test comment in blocked_email_spec.rb documents last_match_at as the signal for 'ever been blocked', which the side-effect placement corrupts.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows EmailValidator calling `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` (lib/validators/email_validator.rb), and `should_block?` mutates state by incrementing `match_count` and setting `last_match_at` on every call (app/models/blocked_email.rb). Because this is inside a validator, it will run on any validation pass where the email matches and earlier errors are blank, not strictly on a single “real signup attempt”. This can plausibly inflate the statistics and blur the meaning of `last_match_at` as an “ever matched/blocked” signal (noted in the blocked_email_spec comment). However, the exact degree of inflation (double-validations, future models using the validator) isn’t directly provable from the diff, so it’s more of an architectural/data-quality concern than a guaranteed functional defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] should_block? mutates and saves the record inside a predicate invoked from validation, so a query-shaped method performs a synchronous write on every email validation. Any code path that validates a user with a changed email (admin edits, updates from other controllers) now silently issues an UPDATE on blocked_emails; a failed save inside validation raises inside the validation pass and surfaces as an opaque validation error, and the write happens even when the validation result is discarded (e.g. .invalid? probes).

adjudication.rationale: Diff shows `EmailValidator#validate_each` calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` during email validation (lib/validators/email_validator.rb), and `should_block?` does a `match_count += 1`, sets `last_match_at`, and calls `record.save` (app/models/blocked_email.rb). This makes a predicate-style validation check perform a synchronous DB write whenever a matching BlockedEmail row exists, including for any `.valid?/.invalid?` probes and any code path that triggers email validation. However, the finding’s claim that a failed save would raise inside validation isn’t supported here because it uses non-bang `save` (no exception by default).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The blocked_emails table is created with no writer anywhere in this diff — no admin UI, API endpoint, rake task, or seed populates it. Operators deploying this feature cannot add a single blocked email without hand-written SQL, so the 'comprehensive email validation for blocked users' the PR promises is inert in production until follow-up work lands; the shipped feature silently does nothing.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `blocked_emails` (migration) and enforcement via `EmailValidator` calling `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`, but there is no code in this diff that creates/maintains `BlockedEmail` records (no controller/admin UI/rake/seed). With an empty table, `should_block?` returns false and the new blocking path never triggers, so the feature requires out-of-band population (e.g., SQL/console). This is a scope/completeness concern rather than a runtime bug in the introduced logic.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The controller echoes back user.attributes including the raw email in `values` on the failure response, and the client pushes only values.email into rejectedEmails without ever clearing that list on modal close. A user who fails signup with a blocked email, closes the modal, changes their mind and types the same address gets a client-side 'invalid' error that can never be cleared by retyping — the stale rejectedEmails entry persists for the controller's lifetime and blocks an address the server may not even reject after an admin unblocks it, until a full page reload.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does introduce a client-side cache of rejected emails: `rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` is checked in `emailValidation()` and will force `failed: true` for any email it contains, and entries are added on failed signup via `rejectedEmails.pushObject(result.values.email)`. There is no code in this diff to ever remove/clear `rejectedEmails` (e.g., on modal close/reset), so if the controller instance is reused, the user cannot clear that client-side invalid state by retyping the same address, and the cache could become stale if server-side blocking changes. However, the claim that it *definitely* persists across modal close can’t be fully verified from this diff alone (controller lifecycle not shown).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] BlockedEmail.should_block? performs a case-sensitive exact-match lookup on an unnormalized email, so a blocked address is trivially bypassed by varying letter case. An admin blocks 'spammer@evil.com'; the spammer registers 'Spammer@evil.com' (or 'SPAMMER@EVIL.COM') and the WHERE email = ... clause on Postgres returns no row, so should_block? returns false and the account is created — the entire feature is defeated by holding the shift key.
matched_golden_ids: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate flags the same underlying issue: `BlockedEmail.should_block?` uses a case-sensitive exact match on unnormalized emails, allowing blocked addresses to bypass the block by changing letter case, leading to unauthorized access/blocked-user signup.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] email_in_restriction_setting? interpolates the raw admin-configured domain string into Regexp.new with no escaping of regex metacharacters, and the resulting pattern is unanchored on the right. A whitelist entry 'gmail.com' builds /@(gmail\.com)/i which matches 'user@gmail.com.attacker.org', letting any attacker-controlled domain pass the whitelist; additionally an entry containing an unbalanced '(' (e.g. 'foo(bar.com') raises RegexpError inside validation, turning every account creation / email change into a 500 until an admin fixes the setting — config is attacker-controllable input (any admin, or a compromised admin panel) feeding a regex sink.
matched_golden_ids: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Yes. Both point to the same underlying flaw: the constructed regex for allowed domains is not properly boundary-anchored, so it can match domains where the whitelisted domain is only a suffix/substring (e.g., example.com matches evil.example.com or gmail.com matches gmail.com.attacker.org), enabling whitelist bypass. The candidate adds additional concerns (regex metacharacter escaping/RegexpError), but it still identifies the golden issue.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] should_block? mutates and saves the BlockedEmail row during model validation, doing a write (with a unique-index conflict risk under concurrency) on every candidate-email validation attempt. Two concurrent signups with the same blocked email race on record.save; on Postgres the second save raises a unique-constraint StatementInvalid, which users_controller rescues only as a generic rescue rendering an opaque error. Unauthenticated attackers also inflate match_count arbitrarily via repeated signup attempts, corrupting the stats the model was built to collect; and the write happens during email-change validation for existing users too, not just signup.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does show that email validation now performs a DB write: `EmailValidator#validate_each` calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`, and `should_block?` increments `match_count`, sets `last_match_at`, and `save`s the row during validation. This will happen on any `User` save where `email_changed?` is true (not just signup), and repeated attempts can inflate these stats. However, the finding’s specific claim that concurrent signups will trigger a *unique index* conflict/`StatementInvalid` on `record.save` is not supported by the diff: `should_block?` only updates an existing row (no insert / no change to the unique `email` column), so a unique-constraint violation from this code path is unlikely; the real concurrency issue here would be lost updates (non-atomic increment), not uniqueness errors.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The email uniqueness validation is now a plain Rails uniqueness check with no case-insensitive scope or downcasing, combined with the removal of the dedicated email_validator method means case-variant duplicate emails are never blocked at the app layer. If the DB unique index on users.email is case-sensitive (Postgres default), 'Bob@x.com' and 'bob@x.com' both validate as unique, producing duplicate accounts for one mailbox — an account-recovery/impersonation foothold for shared-mailbox domains; the index schema is not added or altered in this diff to enforce case-insensitivity.

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes `User` from `validates_uniqueness_of :email` to `validates :email, uniqueness: true`, which is effectively the same default (case-sensitive unless configured). The removed `email_validator` method only enforced domain whitelist/blacklist and is replaced by the new `EmailValidator` (`validates :email, email: true`), not by any case-normalization logic. The finding’s claim that this change newly allows case-variant duplicate emails, and that the DB index behavior is relevant, is not verifiable from this diff and is not shown to be a regression introduced here.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The failure response now echoes user-supplied values (name, username, email) back in the JSON payload, which the client pushes into client-side state and re-displays via the error flash path. Any XSS sink that renders result.values.email or the flash message without escaping turns the signup form into a reflected/stored XSS vector via the server-echoed email field; safe only as long as every consuming template escapes, which this diff does not verify.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does add `values: user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email")` to the JSON failure response (users_controller.rb) and the client stores `result.values.email` in `rejectedEmails` (create_account_controller.js). However, in this diff `result.values.email` is never rendered or flashed back to the user; it is only used in a `.contains(email)` check to short-circuit validation. The flash path uses `result.message` (built from `user.errors.full_messages`), not `result.values.*`. The finding’s claim that the echoed values are re-displayed via the flash path / templates is not verifiable from the shown changes and partially contradicts the client-side code shown.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The EmailValidator spec covers only the BlockedEmail branch of validate_each and leaves the whitelist/blacklist branches (lib/validators/email_validator.rb lines 5-14, the majority of the validator's logic) with zero coverage in this diff. A regression in email_in_restriction_setting? (e.g. the dot-escaping regexp gsub, which is subtle string interpolation into Regexp.new) ships green because the spec suite never constructs a SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist/blacklist case; admins relying on domain restrictions get users signed up from blacklisted domains before anyone notices. Checked spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb and spec/models/blocked_email_spec.rb — neither sets either SiteSetting.

adjudication.rationale: In this diff, `lib/validators/email_validator.rb` introduces nontrivial logic for `SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist` / `email_domains_blacklist` plus the `email_in_restriction_setting?` regexp-building helper (lines 3–21). However, the only new validator spec (`spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb`) exercises only the `BlockedEmail.should_block?` branch by stubbing `BlockedEmail.should_block?` and never sets either `SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist` or `SiteSetting.email_domains_blacklist`. `spec/models/blocked_email_spec.rb` also doesn’t cover SiteSetting behavior. So regressions in the whitelist/blacklist logic could ship without test failure.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Both specs stub BlockedEmail.should_block? with a canned return value, so the test pair is a tautology that verifies only that an if-statement branches on a stubbed boolean — the real BlockedEmail query, the action_type comparison, and the 'user.email.blocked' message are never exercised through the validator. spec/models/blocked_email_spec.rb covers should_block? in isolation, but the wiring between validator and model is never integration-tested: if the validator's errors message key changes or the errors[attribute].blank? guard misfires in the presence of a pre-existing error, these specs still pass while end-to-end blocked-email rejection is broken. The specs also assert only errors present/absent, never the message content, so a wrong I18n key passes.

adjudication.rationale: In spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb both examples stub BlockedEmail.should_block? to return true/false, so the validator spec only checks the conditional branch and never exercises the real BlockedEmail.should_block? logic (query, action_type check, stats update) through the validator. The spec also only asserts errors[:email] present/absent, not that the specific I18n message/key (user.email.blocked) was added, and it doesn’t cover the `record.errors[attribute].blank?` guard behavior when another email error already exists. This is a diff-grounded test coverage gap rather than a runtime defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] No test exercises the combined branch where a whitelist/blacklist error is already present so BlockedEmail.should_block? is short-circuited (lib/validators/email_validator.rb line 15 'if record.errors[attribute].blank and ...'), meaning the behavioral side effect — match_count not incremented and last_match_at not updated when the domain restriction fires first — is unverified. Site operators loading the blocked_emails table to track which blocked addresses are being attempted (the explicit rationale in the last_match_at spec comment) get silently wrong statistics for any email that also trips a domain restriction, and no spec fails to reveal it. Checked both spec files in the diff; neither creates a record with both a domain restriction error and a blocked email.

adjudication.rationale: In `lib/validators/email_validator.rb`, `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` is only called when `record.errors[attribute].blank?` (line with `if record.errors[attribute].blank? and ...`). That means if a whitelist/blacklist restriction adds an error first (`user.email.not_allowed`), the blocked-email check is skipped and its side effects (incrementing `match_count`, setting `last_match_at` in `BlockedEmail.should_block?`) won’t occur. The added specs (`spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb` and `spec/models/blocked_email_spec.rb`) cover blocked vs not blocked, but do not exercise the combined case where a domain restriction error is present and thus short-circuits the blocked-email path. This is a concrete, diff-grounded test/edge-case gap around newly added behavior/side effects, though whether it’s a “bug” depends on intended semantics.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new blocked_emails table has no writer anywhere in this diff, and its action_type column is NOT NULL with no database default. Operators who want to use the feature must hand-load rows via SQL (the spec comment explicitly anticipates 'manually load the table'), and any raw INSERT that omits action_type fails on the NOT NULL constraint because the default only exists in the model's before_validation callback; meanwhile no admin UI/API exists to populate the table, so the feature ships inert.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a `blocked_emails` table (migration) and reads it via `BlockedEmail.should_block?` in the new `EmailValidator`, but introduces no UI/API/admin pathway to create/manage `BlockedEmail` rows—only specs and a fabricator create records. So operationally the feature only does anything if rows are populated out-of-band (e.g., Rails console/manual DB work), making it effectively inert by default. However, the finding’s claim that operators “must hand-load rows via SQL” is overstated: creating records through the Rails model will set `action_type` via `before_validation :set_defaults`, avoiding the NOT NULL issue; the NOT NULL/no DB default only bites for raw SQL inserts omitting `action_type`.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] BlockedEmail.should_block? performs a read-modify-write save inside a validation path, and is invoked from EmailValidator on every email_changed? validation. Every signup validation run (including repeated .valid? calls in one request or controller) increments match_count and issues an UPDATE, so statistics are double-counted and a hot signup path gains an unconditional DB write per attempt; a failure of that save (e.g., unique-index race) raises inside validation and turns a rejection into a 500.

adjudication.rationale: Diff shows `EmailValidator#validate_each` calling `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` during model validation (lib/validators/email_validator.rb), and `should_block?` performs a side-effecting `match_count += 1`, `last_match_at = Time.zone.now`, and `record.save` (app/models/blocked_email.rb). Because validations can be invoked multiple times (e.g., repeated `.valid?` / `.save` attempts), this can double-count matches and adds an extra UPDATE on a hot path whenever a blocked email record exists. However, the finding’s claim about a “unique-index race” raising inside validation is not directly supported here: it uses `save` (non-bang) and updates an existing row, so uniqueness violations are unlikely from this code alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] BlockedEmail lookup matches the raw email string exactly with no normalization, while email_in_restriction_setting? uses a case-insensitive regexp. A user entering Blocked@Spammers.org when the table contains blocked@spammers.org is accepted (no match), so manually-loaded blocklists silently miss case variants; also, since case-insensitive uniqueness on users.email elsewhere in the codebase means the same person registers the same address in different casing, the blocklist is only as good as the exact string loaded.

adjudication.rationale: In the new blocked-email path, `EmailValidator` calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` and `should_block?` does an exact equality lookup (`BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first`) with no normalization (no downcasing/stripping) and no case-insensitive query. By contrast, the domain whitelist/blacklist check explicitly builds a case-insensitive regexp (`Regexp.new(..., true)`). From the diff, nothing normalizes `user.email` before validation, so a casing variant like `Blocked@Spammers.org` would not match a stored `blocked@spammers.org` on case-sensitive DBs (e.g., Postgres), causing the blocklist to be bypassed.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] BlockedEmail.should_block? performs a stateful DB write (incrementing match_count, setting last_match_at, record.save) inside User's validation pass, so the write runs on every validation, not on the actual blocked event. A single failed signup for a blocked email gets counted once per validation pass (validations run multiple times across form re-submissions and other code paths that call valid?/save), inflating match_count and rewriting last_match_at; additionally, since should_block? is invoked from validate_each, the UPDATE executes inside the surrounding user-save transaction and is silently rolled back when the user creation fails for any other reason — the stats write is silently dropped (record.save's return value is never checked) with no log or error.

adjudication.rationale: In `lib/validators/email_validator.rb`, `validate_each` calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` when the email has no prior email-attribute errors. `BlockedEmail.should_block?` (new `app/models/blocked_email.rb`) performs a DB write (`match_count += 1`, `last_match_at = ...`, `record.save`) as a side effect of validation. Since validations can run multiple times per attempted signup (e.g., repeated submissions / multiple `valid?`/`save` calls), this will increment `match_count` and update `last_match_at` on each validation pass rather than strictly on a single “blocked event,” inflating the stats. The additional claim about the write being inside the user-save transaction/rolled back is not directly verifiable from the diff, but the core issue (stateful DB mutation during validation leading to repeated/inaccurate counting) is clearly present.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The match_count increment uses read-modify-write (record.match_count += 1; record.save) with no locking, so concurrent signup attempts for the same blocked email lose increments. Operators relying on match_count to gauge spam pressure under-count under concurrency (two simultaneous requests both read count=5, both write 6); also the concurrent saves can collide on updated_at/last_match_at, last write wins. Low impact for stats, but the counter's purpose (measuring abuse volume) is exactly the workload where concurrency occurs.

adjudication.rationale: In `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, the code does `record.match_count += 1; record.last_match_at = Time.zone.now; record.save` after `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first`. This is a classic read-modify-write pattern without any locking/atomic update, so concurrent calls for the same `email` can lose increments (both read the same `match_count` and write back the same incremented value). Likewise, `last_match_at`/`updated_at` updates are last-write-wins under concurrency. This behavior is directly present in the diff and can cause incorrect statistics under concurrent signups.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The client-side rejectedEmails check only fires after a failed submit and displays the generic I18n.t('user.email.invalid') message rather than the server's specific 'user.email.blocked' message delivered in result.errors.email. A user whose email is blocked on a retry sees 'invalid' (generic format message) instead of the server's 'is not allowed.' message that was already returned in the payload, misleading the user into thinking they typo'd the address and retrying format changes that can never succeed.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a client-side cache `rejectedEmails` and, on retry, `emailValidation` returns a failure with `reason: I18n.t('user.email.invalid')` whenever the email is in that list (create_account_controller.js: new `rejectedEmails` + `contains(email)` branch). On submit failure, the controller pushes `result.values.email` into `rejectedEmails` when `result.errors.email` is present (create_account_controller.js). Since the server now returns structured `errors` (users_controller.rb) and can specifically add `user.email.blocked` (email_validator.rb + locale `user.email.blocked`), the client is indeed discarding that more specific server reason and replacing it with a generic “invalid” message on subsequent validations, which is misleading behavior introduced by this change.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The create-failure response now unconditionally includes user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email"), echoing the user's raw submitted email back in every failed-signup response regardless of which field failed. Callers get the submitted email echoed even when the failure was a username/password error, which the client only consumes on email errors; more importantly the response payload grows per-request with unvalidated input on an unauthenticated endpoint (previously only the message was returned). Minor, but it is a new unbounded-ish echo of raw input on the public signup path.

adjudication.rationale: In `app/controllers/users_controller.rb#create`, the failure branch now always renders `errors: user.errors.to_hash` and `values: user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email")` alongside the message. This unconditionally echoes back the submitted `email` (and other fields) on every failed signup, regardless of which field failed, whereas previously only `message` was returned. The diff also shows the client only uses this for email rejections (`create_account_controller.js` checks `result.errors.email` then pushes `result.values.email`), so returning `values` for all failures is extra surface/payload on a public unauthenticated endpoint.
